review.translation: [Now it happened|0] [in the days of|1] [Amraphel|2] [king of|3] [Shinar|4], [Arioch|5] [king of|6] [Ellasar|7], [Chedorlaomer|8] [king of|9] [Elam|10], [and Tidal|11] [king of|12] [the Goiim|13],

analysis.evidence: וַיְהִי introduces the narrative. The following phrase בִּימֵי, “in the days of,” dates the event by naming the four kings.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks יְהִי, the short third-person masculine singular Qal form of הָיָה, as a wayyiqtol. The verb is used impersonally.

analysis.evidence: אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר identifies Amraphel as king of Shinar. בִּימֵי dates the narrative to the time of his reign.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition בִּ means “in” or “during.” ימֵי is the masculine plural construct of יוֹם, with אַמְרָפֶל as its complement.
analysis.sense: (pl.) days of a life, a reign or an age

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:9 as evidence identifying the same bearer.
draft.definition: Amraphel, the king of Shinar. The meaning of his name is unknown.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:9 repeats the name and royal title found in Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר, “king of Shinar,” identifies אַמְרָפֶל. The same pattern recurs in אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר, “Arioch, king of Ellasar.” The verse gives no basis for assigning the name to the root אמר.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun, a personal name with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר identifies Amraphel as king of Shinar. The verse repeats the same title for each of the next three rulers. The source gloss “their heart” conflicts with both the title and the absence of a possessive suffix.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a place-name entry for Shinar under its own consonants. The source gloss “ewe” and proposed root שנס lack support here.
draft.definition: Shinar is the land in which Genesis 10:10 locates Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh.
draft.evidence: The phrase בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר identifies the region containing the four cities.

analysis.evidence: אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר means “Amraphel, king of Shinar.” The parallel title אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר, “Arioch, king of Ellasar,” confirms that שִׁנְעָר names a territory.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It follows the construct noun מֶלֶךְ and names Amraphel’s realm.
analysis.sense: The land containing Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh.

draft.definition: Arioch, the personal name of the king of Ellasar. Its meaning is uncertain.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:9 repeats the name and royal title אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר from Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר, “king of Ellasar,” identifies אַרְיוֹךְ in the same name-and-title pattern as אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר. Genesis 14:9 repeats the same name and title. The text supplies no basis for assigning the root ארח.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal proper noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר identifies Arioch as king of Ellasar. The place name אֶלָּסָר completes the construct phrase and names the realm he rules.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a place-name entry with the gloss “Ellasar” and correct the source gloss “emptiness; vanity.”
draft.definition: Ellasar is the place named as Arioch’s realm in Genesis 14:1.
draft.evidence: The title אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר identifies Arioch as king of Ellasar.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 14:1 calls Arioch מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר just as it calls Amraphel מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר. Each place name identifies the realm of the preceding king.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It completes the construct phrase מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר, “king of Ellasar.”

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם, “king of Elam,” immediately follows כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר. This follows the same name-and-title pattern as אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר earlier in the verse. The verse gives no evidence for deriving the name from כדר.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The initial כְּ belongs to the name. The form has no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The verse pairs each king with his realm. In כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם, עֵילָם names Chedorlaomer’s realm, just as שִׁנְעָר names Amraphel’s.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It completes the construct phrase מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם, “king of Elam.”
analysis.sense: Elam, the kingdom ruled by Chedorlaomer

draft.definition: Tidal, the personal name of the king of Goyim.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:1 identifies Tidal by the title מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם immediately after his name.

analysis.evidence: Each of the preceding three names is followed by מֶלֶךְ and the name of the ruler’s realm. וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם completes the list and identifies Tidal as king of Goyim. The verse gives no etymology for his name.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ ‘and’ introduces the personal name תִּדְעָל. After the vocal shewa of וְ, the initial ת appears without dagesh.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 69121:3, 69121:6, 69121:9.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Append the proper noun גּוֹיִם under גוה and assign it the Goyim key already identified in the article’s note.
draft.definition: Goyim is the designation of Tidal’s realm in his royal title.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:1 places Goyim alongside Shinar, Ellasar, and Elam in a list of royal titles. Genesis 14:9 repeats Tidal’s title.

analysis.evidence: The verse pairs each king with his realm. After “king of Shinar,” “king of Ellasar,” and “king of Elam,” מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם identifies Tidal in the same way. The form also reads literally as “nations.” The parallel titles favor Goyim as a designation for his realm, whose location the verse leaves unspecified.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with the masculine plural form of גּוֹי. It stands after the construct מֶלֶךְ and has no prefix or pronominal suffix.
